source: Wang et al. (2026) Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making (UIST 2026)
finding: Built a tool that turns LLM rationales into argument maps (conclusion, premises, support, objections). Graphs helped people catch AI errors on verbal reasoning but hurt on visual reasoning.
numbers: Online study, N=204 valid (223 recruited, Prolific), 2x2 between-subjects (graph vs text x verbal BBH vs visual I-RAVEN). Rationales from GPT-5.4 high effort. Format x modality interaction significant on all 4 trust metrics (Appropriate Trust p<.001; Over-Trust p=.005; Error Correction p<.001).
limits: Single study, online lay participants, one tool design. The graph is generated by the same LLM that may be wrong.
agent_relevance: Argument-map output is a task-class tool: use for verbal logical tasks, not for perceptual or visual ones. Fits S2 scoped to a task class.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making (UIST 2026)
finding: On verbal reasoning (BBH) the graph benefit appeared only on hard questions. Easy questions showed no gain.
numbers: Hard BBH: Over-Trust beta=-0.199 (p=.002), Error Correction beta=+0.182 (p=.002). Collapsed over difficulty: Over-Trust -0.144 (p=.033), Error Correction +0.127 (p=.040). Easy: not significant.
quote: explicit argument structure helps only when reasoning demands are sufficiently high
limits: Effects are on user trust calibration (do people accept wrong AI answers), not on model accuracy.
agent_relevance: Gate the map step by difficulty: skip on easy items, use on hard ones.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making (UIST 2026)
finding: On visual reasoning (I-RAVEN) the graph made calibration worse at both difficulty levels, even though users liked it more.
numbers: Appropriate Trust beta=-0.165 (p<.001), Under-Trust +0.186 (p<.001), Error Correction -0.233 (p<.001). Satisfaction +0.74, Engagement +0.99, Helpfulness +0.68 (all p<.03). On verbal BBH the subjective pattern was reversed: Satisfaction -0.76, Usability -0.72, Learning Gain -0.82.
quote: the format that better supports calibrated decisions is not the one users prefer
limits: Subjective and objective results split. Need for cognition moderates: high-NFC users gained more on verbal.
agent_relevance: Do not trust self-reported helpfulness of a map. Judge by outcome. Do not force a graph on visual tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making (UIST 2026)
finding: Quality audit of the GPT-5.4 argument maps: structure was reliable, but errors in wrong-answer rationales were mostly wrong sub-conclusions or hallucinated evidence.
numbers: 180 rationales: 5 structural issues (2.8%), Cohen's kappa 0.94. Correct answers (n=120): redundant steps 13%, unverifiable claims 8%. Incorrect answers (n=60): problematic or hallucinated evidence 43%, incorrect sub-conclusions 50%, missing evidence 17%.
limits: Prompt was iteratively refined by the authors; counts are from the final prompt only.
agent_relevance: A map makes each flawed step a separate node, a checkable target for a verifier pass.

source: Wang et al. (2026) Graphionale: How Graph Visualizations of LLM Rationales Affect Human Decision Making (UIST 2026) (formative co-design part)
finding: Co-design users wanted small maps: 3-4 layers, 3-5 nodes per layer, colour for support versus reject, collapsible branches.
numbers: 10 participants, sessions of about 25 minutes. Challenge themes: node text overload, hard interpretation of relations, navigation cost on large diagrams.
limits: Small formative study, no effect test.
agent_relevance: Cap map size. Large maps overload readers and verifiers.

source: Pirozelli et al. (2026) An LLM-Based System for Argument Mining (ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of LLMs)
finding: A multi-stage LLM pipeline (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5-mini) rebuilds argument graphs (premise, conclusion; support, attack, undercut) from text. On textbook arguments it scores well against gold diagrams.
numbers: Textbook arguments: conclusion detection accuracy 92.50%; span precision 80.31, recall 72.87, F1 75.70; relation accuracy 80.57% (only items with at least two matching components).
limits: The PDF table is garbled, so row-to-metric mapping is read from the discussion text. Single fixed seed; authors report large run-to-run variability in structure.
agent_relevance: LLMs can map short clear arguments reliably. Sample several maps and keep the most coherent one, as the authors suggest.

source: Pirozelli et al. (2026) An LLM-Based System for Argument Mining (ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of LLMs)
finding: Expert raters judged structure well: implicit premises, undercuts, and linked versus convergent premises were mostly right.
numbers: Two annotators, 1-3 scale: implicit premises M=2.86 (exact agreement .95), undercuts M=2.90 (.88), convergent/linked M=2.85 (.80). Only eight arguments contained undercuts.
limits: Small textbook set. Undercut judgement relied on counterfactual reasoning, so agreement is weaker.
agent_relevance: Implicit-premise recovery works on short texts. Test it on longer ones before relying on it.

source: Pirozelli et al. (2026) An LLM-Based System for Argument Mining (ICLR 2026 Workshop on Logical Reasoning of LLMs)
finding: On real benchmark corpora the full pipeline is poor, mainly because it cannot select exact spans. With gold spans, relation prediction beats the old state of the art on AbstRCT.
numbers: Full pipeline AbstRCT span F1 59.65 vs Morio et al. 2022 at 70.93; component macro-F1 27.64 vs 64.78. AAEC full pipeline link F1 0.41 vs 55.72. Gold components on AbstRCT: link 51.51 (+11.77 over baseline), relation 46.21 (+7.5). AAEC with gold components: relation still below baseline (22.88 vs 55.72).
limits: Exact-match scoring punishes valid alternative segmentations. Table text partly garbled.
agent_relevance: Span choice is the weak step; links are strong once nodes are given. Let the agent choose nodes freely and judge links.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: ArgLLMs: the LLM writes one supporting and one attacking argument per claim (depth 1 or 2), scores each, and a formal bipolar argumentation framework (DF-QuAD or QE) computes the claim strength. Accuracy was about the same as chain of thought.
numbers: Three claim datasets (TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim from TruthfulQA, StrategyQA, MedQA). Eight LLMs, e.g. Mistral, Mixtral, Gemma 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4o. Accuracy mostly 0.5-0.85 depending on model and dataset. Direct question, CoT, and ArgLLM with estimated base score were best. Depth 2 means seven arguments.
limits: Authors note limited zero-shot argument generation and strength estimation, and large prompt sensitivity in the pilot. No consistent gain over CoT.
agent_relevance: A direct agent-loop use of an argument map: build a pro and con tree, score nodes, compute the verdict by rule. Gives an auditable decision where one node can be contested.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) Argumentative Large Language Models for Explainable and Contestable Claim Verification (AAAI 2025)
finding: The authors argue a CoT rationale may not cause the answer, while an ArgLLM answer is fixed by its argument graph. They define formal contestability properties.
numbers: Formal properties shown; no human contestability study. Accuracy comparison as above.
quote: the final decision outputted by ArgLLMs is faithfully determined by the arguments and the argumentation semantics
limits: Faithful only for the aggregation step, not for how the LLM scores each argument.
agent_relevance: Aggregate by rule over mapped arguments so the last step is inspectable.

source: Crudele and Raffaghelli (2025) Argument mapping and ChatGPT as mediational tools for argumentative skills (Je-LKS)
finding: Tiny quasi-experiment combining argument mapping with ChatGPT. The multimodal map group did best. ChatGPT alone beat analog-text maps but was weaker on advanced argument reworking.
numbers: N=17 female undergraduates, University of Padua, three groups: G1 maps with analog texts, G2 maps with multimodal texts, G3 ChatGPT only (control). G2 critical-thinking score 7.25/10 at both CT1 and CT4. Only G3 fell significantly below the reference on general opinion level.
limits: Case study, not randomized, one sex, groups of about 5-10. Authors do not claim statistical generalisation.
agent_relevance: Weak hint that a map plus structured LLM dialogue beats free chat. Not enough to base a design on.

source: Anastasiou and De Liddo (2024) A Hybrid Human-AI Approach for Argument Map Creation From Transcripts (DELITE)
finding: Proposes an LLM pass that turns deliberation transcripts into IBIS-style maps (positions, pro and con, with timestamps), then human curation. Model quality differed a lot in one demo.
numbers: Qualitative demo on a European Parliament transcript: GPT-3.5 gave the simplest map; GPT-4 and Gemini Advanced were better; Gemini Advanced ignored the format and omitted all con arguments. Hypotheses H1 (model matters) and H2 (human curation helps) stated, not tested.
limits: Position paper, no metrics.
agent_relevance: Schema non-compliance (dropping cons) is a failure mode. Add a check that attack nodes exist.

source: Buckingham Shum (2024) Generative AI for Critical Analysis: Practical Tools, Cognitive Offloading and Human Agency (GenAILA)
finding: Bing Chat could not draw an argument map directly but wrote Argdown code that rendered one. The map held two kinds of hallucination: invented argument schemes and a summary node about content the source never states.
numbers: One worked example on one article; no numbers. Invented schemes named: Argument from responsibility, Argument from precaution.
limits: Anecdote. Suggests students critique AI-made maps as a task.
agent_relevance: Hallucinated nodes look rigorous in map form. Each node needs a source-grounding check. Argdown text is an easy map output format.

source: UMSL thesis (2025) LLM argument maps from student essays with few-shot prompting
finding: Web app made argument maps from student essays by few-shot prompting. Edge cases (prompt hijack, single phrase, deliberately contradictory arguments) caused hallucination. Evaluation was qualitative.
numbers: No numbers seen. Known only from a search result snippet.
limits: Not opened. Thesis, small scale.
agent_relevance: Auto-mapping tools need input validation and contradiction handling.

source: Shi et al. (2026) Tackling the Root of Misinformation by Teaching Laypeople about Logical Fallacies via Socratic Questioning and Critical Argumentation (LFTutor)
finding: LFTutor, a scaffolded tutor with intent-driven Socratic strategy choice and strategy verification, beat a plain GPT-4o tutor and a prompt-patched one on dialogue quality. Just telling the model to avoid known failures was not enough.
numbers: Normal students: above BASE by up to 53% on average and up to 85% per metric; above BASE-with-problems by 23% on average. Adversarial student: Divergence 84.0 vs 38.0, Stance Change 82.0 vs 11.9. Pilot of plain LLM tutors: concession to student stance in 85% of dialogues, divergence 35%, strategy fixation 90%.
limits: About argument quality tutoring, not map drawing. Automatic judge is QwQ-32B. Backbone GPT-4o; Gemini-2.5-pro and Llama-3.1 gave broadly consistent results.
agent_relevance: A verified, step-by-step critical-argument procedure resists persuasion better than instructions. Relevant to sycophancy guards.

source: Shi et al. (2026) Tackling the Root of Misinformation by Teaching Laypeople about Logical Fallacies via Socratic Questioning and Critical Argumentation (LFTutor)
finding: Human check of LFTutor: 20 participants rated it significantly better than the baseline on 8 of 9 metrics.
numbers: N=20 fluent English speakers, Likert 1-5; one-sided t-tests; significant at p<0.05 for strategy-related items; example mean 3.35 vs 4.15 (+0.8) on one metric.
limits: Small sample, short sessions.
agent_relevance: Human ratings agree with the automatic judge here, giving some trust in LLM-judge evaluation of argument tutors.

source: Pal Chowdhury et al. (2024) Enhancing Critical Thinking in Education by means of a Socratic Chatbot
finding: Fine and prompt tuned Llama2 7B and 13B as a Socratic tutor. With simulated students it was rated as supporting reflection and critical thinking better than standard chatbots.
numbers: Simulated student, 20 conversations of 5 turns each, METEOR and critical-thinking measures. Exact gains not extracted this session.
limits: No real students; small open models; no argument map.
agent_relevance: Socratic scaffolding is a thin cousin of map training. No map-specific evidence.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Graph of Verification: Structured Verification of LLM Reasoning with Directed Acyclic Graphs
finding: Turn a reasoning chain into a DAG of blocks, verify each block with only its premises, and flag the first wrong step. Beats one-pass whole-chain checking, with the biggest gains on hard sets.
numbers: ProcessBench F1 (holistic to GoV): Qwen2.5-32B OlympiadBench 35.9 to 65.2, GSM8K 59.8 to 78.1, MATH 49.4 to 72.7. Qwen2.5-72B GSM8K 75.6 to 80.3. Llama3.3-70B GSM8K 78.6 to 78.6 (no change).
limits: Math reasoning, not natural argument. It is a step DAG, not a map with attacks. Gains vary by model.
agent_relevance: Closest evidence that a graph view of the model's own reasoning helps a verifier by keeping context small per node.

source: Fang et al. (2025) Graph of Verification: Structured Verification of LLM Reasoning with Directed Acyclic Graphs
finding: On a synthetic triangle-sum task the DAG verifier held up as problems grew, while holistic checking collapsed.
numbers: F1 at problem size N=8: Qwen2.5-7B 51.5 to 70.7; Qwen2.5-14B 62.9 to 86.8; Qwen2.5-32B 56.3 to 91.4.
limits: Synthetic arithmetic with injected errors (50% corruption chance); may not carry to natural arguments.
agent_relevance: Decomposed per-node checks scale better with chain length.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Mapping the Minds of LLMs: A Graph-Based Analysis of Reasoning LLM
finding: Reasoning traces of reasoning models parsed into directed graphs. Denser, more branching, more converging graphs go with higher accuracy. Prompts forcing linear structure lower accuracy.
numbers: Pearson r with accuracy: exploration density 0.68, branching 0.67, convergence 0.68 (all p<.05). Accuracy zero-shot vs concise vs explanatory few-shot: Llama-8B 44.5/41.2/32.7; Qwen-14B 51.8/48.5/45.3; Qwen3-32B 56.2/53.7/50.1.
limits: Correlation across few conditions. Describes trace graphs, not argument maps in the van Gelder sense.
agent_relevance: Favours scaffolds that branch and then merge, not rigid linear templates.

source: Large Language Models in Argument Mining: A Survey (2025)
finding: Survey of LLMs for argument mining. In-context GPT-4 can match fine-tuned RoBERTa on argument quality; CoT plus voting adds gains; LLM judges show biases.
numbers: With three exemplars GPT-4 matches or beats fine-tuned RoBERTa on GAQCorpus convincingness and sufficiency; CoT with self-consistency over five traces gave +7 macro-F1 on IBM-Rank; RAG-GPT-4 +3 sufficiency F1 on AMELIA legal.
limits: Secondary summary; figures quoted from the survey, not checked in the originals. Survey says implicit premises and cross-topic robustness remain hard.
agent_relevance: Self-consistency over several maps is a cheap gain. Implicit premises are the known hole.

source: Bhatia et al. (2026) Guided Sensemaking: Agents in Collaborative Deliberation
finding: A Reflector agent parses a writer's text into a live claim and evidence graph while a Socratic Guide agent asks questions. The method sits inside an LLM loop but has no results yet.
numbers: No empirical numbers. Authors list a learning-gain evaluation as future work.
limits: System description only.
agent_relevance: Template for a two-agent loop: one agent maps, another questions gaps in the map.

source: Dung (1995) On the acceptability of arguments and its fundamental role in nonmonotonic reasoning
finding: Abstract argumentation frameworks: arguments plus attack relations with extension semantics. Base for ArgLLMs and many argument-graph systems.
numbers: Not opened this session; background knowledge.
limits: Not opened. Cited in the opened Pirozelli paper.
agent_relevance: Formal rule for settling an attack graph after the model maps it.

source: Older argument mapping software: Araucaria, Rationale, Carneades, Argdown
finding: Older tools: Araucaria (annotation), Rationale (classroom mapping tool), Carneades (formal evaluation), Argdown (markup rendered to maps, used by Bing Chat in the Buckingham Shum example).
numbers: Not opened; no numbers.
limits: Background only.
agent_relevance: Argdown-style text markup is a cheap way for an LLM to emit a map.

source: Gap note: no study found that tests LLMs on van Gelder-style argument-mapping training outcomes (critical thinking test gains)
finding: Across 6 web searches and API queries, no controlled study measured whether an LLM improves on critical-thinking tests after map-style prompting, or compared LLM versus human map quality with effect sizes.
numbers: None found. Closest: Graphionale (N=204, human decisions), ArgLLMs (accuracy parity with CoT), Crudele (N=17).
limits: Semantic Scholar and arXiv APIs rate-limited or returned nothing; search was thin.
agent_relevance: Map step for the agent is supported by indirect evidence only. Test it on our own benchmarks before adopting.
